chunk_findings.detail: `_set_legacy_ids` renders each derived item's legacy id with a raw `IDS.render(...)` and never re-applies `_unique`, so the legacy id does not include the suffix the old import actually assigned to a colliding item. `_keep_imported_ids` then renames every scanned item whose legacy id is `in known`, without checking that the assigned id is still unique among the scanned items. Concretely, a file whose old import produced two ids from the same text — e.g. an old queue containing `PHASE-ONE.do-thing` and `PHASE-ONE.do-thing-2` for two identical checklist lines `- [ ] Do thing` (the old scan used `_unique`, which appends `-2`; the code under review even relies on this device in `_adopt_child_prefix`: `t.ident = _unique("", f"{best}.{t.ident[len(old_ident) + 1 :]}", taken)`). On re-import with the new word-boundary slugs, both tasks get `old_slug` = `do-thing`, hence the same `legacy_ident = "PHASE-ONE.do-thing"`. Both satisfy `old in known and f.ident not in known`, so both get `f.ident = "PHASE-ONE.do-thing"`. Two distinct `Found` entries now carry one id: `_triage_found` will match both scanned entries to (at best) the single existing `PHASE-ONE.do-thing` queue item, and the existing `PHASE-ONE.do-thing-2` item is never matched — so the two checklist items are merged/collapsed or the second one is duplicated, which is exactly the re-import corruption the change is meant to prevent. The same gap applies to phases: two identical phase headings get the same `legacy_ident`, so the second phase can be renamed onto the first phase's id.

chunk_findings.detail: `_title_of` splits on `_SENTENCE_END = re.compile(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+(?=[A-Z0-9`\"'(\[])")`, which treats a leading list ordinal "N." as the end of a sentence, because the period is followed by whitespace and a capital. Its docstring promises "a title that is a whole phrase: the first sentence of `text` when it fits". For the exact heading shape in this bug report, `_title_of("39. Follow-ups not followed up")` returns `"39."`: the lookbehind matches the `.` after `39`, `\s+` eats the space, the lookahead sees the capital `F`, so `first = "39."`, `len("39.") <= 120` and the whole remainder of the heading is discarded. The same happens for any numbered item ("1. Add the base room to blueprints" → title `"1."`), which is precisely how imported markdown headings/bullets are written (this project's own headings are `39. ...`, `142.A ...`). The item keeps all the text in its body, but the title/id surface becomes `39.`, i.e. the "unwieldy / not readable" symptom the change set out to fix is re-introduced via the title path. The sentence splitter needs to exclude an ordinal/abbreviation context (e.g. require the token before the punctuation to be a real word, or ignore `\d+\.` at the start), otherwise `_title_of` returns a fragment instead of a phrase for numbered items.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer.py (`_SENTENCE_END` / `_title_of`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`legacy_ident` is computed as a raw re-render of the old-rule id — for tasks `IDS.render(..., phase=old_phase, slug=_slug(unsplit or body, _OLD_TASK_SLUG))`, for phases `old_derived` — but the id the old importer actually stored was `_unique(ident, derived, taken)`, which appends a disambiguator when two items derive the same truncated id. Because this whole change exists to handle the old 20/24-char `_slug` cut, truncated-id collisions are exactly the common case, and ignoring `_unique` makes the "legacy" ids non-unique.

Concrete repro: a queue produced by the old code from a file where two task titles slugify to the same first 20 chars (e.g. "give base room blue paint" and "give base room blue primer" → both `P42.8.give-base-room-blue`). The queue therefore holds `P42.8.give-base-room-blue` and `P42.8.give-base-room-blue-2`. On re-import, `_set_legacy_ids` assigns *both* scanned tasks the same `legacy_ident` `P42.8.give-base-room-blue`; in `_keep_imported_ids` both satisfy `old in known and f.ident not in known`, so both get `f.ident = old`. Two distinct scanned items now carry one ident, and the second overwrites/is dropped instead of being matched to `…-2` — silent data loss. The same happens for phases: two headings such as "39. Follow-ups not verified" and "39. Follow-ups not applicable" both set `legacy_ident = "PHASE-39-FOLLOW-UPS-NOT"`, and the phase loop (`if f.kind == "phase" and old and old in known and f.ident not in known: renamed[f.ident] = old; f.ident = old`) renames both phases to that one id, collapsing them (and their children).

Fix needs to reconstruct the disambiguated old id (or make `_keep_imported_ids` claim ids it has already assigned in this pass, skipping a legacy id that is taken by a different scanned item).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer.py:_set_legacy_ids (and `_keep_imported_ids`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new guard is written against a `word` that always carries the closing punctuation, so its `[A-Za-z]` alternative is unreachable and the single-letter case named in the code's own comment (`39.` / `A.` / `e.g.`) is not handled.

Why the punctuation is always attached: the companion test in this same diff asserts `IM._title_of("Fix it, e.g. Foo bar. Then more") == "Fix it, e.g. Foo bar."`. Since the code does `first = text[: m.start()]` with no re-appended punctuation, `m.start()` must be the whitespace *after* the `.` (i.e. `_SENTENCE_END` is a look-behind form such as `(?<=[.!?])\s+`). Consequently `word = text[: m.start()].rsplit(" ", 1)[-1]` is the last token *including* the terminating `.`/`!`/`?`. `[\d.]+` matches `"39."` and `(?:[A-Za-z]\.){2,}` matches `"e.g."`, but `[A-Za-z]` fullmatches only a bare letter and can never match a token whose last character is a punctuation mark — it is dead code.

Demonstration: `_title_of("A. Follow-ups not followed up")` → the only `_SENTENCE_END` match is the whitespace after `A.`, `word == "A."` → `re.fullmatch(r"[\d.]+|[A-Za-z]|(?:[A-Za-z]\.){2,}", "A.")` is `None` → not skipped → `first = "A."` → `len(first) <= limit` → returns `"A."`. Same for `"I. Do the thing"` → `"I."`, and `"a. first item"` → `"a."`. The phase is then minted with the slug `a`, i.e. exactly the truncated/unwieldy-id failure B5d57136281 is supposed to fix, for the very input class the comment claims to have covered (`A.` should have matched some `[A-Za-z]\.`-style alternative).
